title: The full-moon night
hookLine: on a full-moon night a monk asks about the five heaps

lines: QUESTIONS PEOPLE ONLY ASK AT NIGHT
cards: Some conversations only happen outside, at night. Phones down, a porch or a rooftop, the moon bright enough to see faces. People ask things there they'd never ask at noon.

The hundred and ninth discourse happens on a night like that: the observance day of the fifteenth, the full moon. The Buddha sits in the open air at the Eastern Park near Savatthi, the monks around him.
One monk stands, arranges his robe over one shoulder, and asks if he may put a question. He has more than one.

teach.b: His questions are all about the five heaps, the khandhas: body, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness, the bundles a person seems to be made of. Are these the five heaps we cling to? Yes.
What are they rooted in? Desire.
Then a sharp one: is the clinging the same as the heaps, or apart from them? Neither, the Buddha says. The clinging is the desire and lust for them.
The heaps are just heaps; the trouble is the grabbing. Why call them heaps? Because each gathers everything of its kind: past, future and present, near and far, coarse and subtle.
Body rests on the four elements. Feeling, perception and formations rest on contact. Consciousness rests on name-and-form.
And a sense of self gets built by taking any heap as me, or mine, or my self. Then a twist.
Another monk has a quiet worry: if there's no self, who receives the results of my deeds? The Buddha knows the thought.
He warns that someone driven by craving might try to outrun the teaching this way, then turns it back into questions. Is body permanent or impermanent? Impermanent.
Is what's impermanent worth calling me? No.
The text closes saying that as he spoke, sixty monks were freed.
Look back at the week: a way to Brahma through boundless kindness, an arrow-maker's warmth, meaning over wording, disputes settled, a path shown, a teaching for refuge.
And now the five heaps, under a full moon.

how: In many Buddhist countries the full-moon observance day (uposatha, or poya in Sri Lanka) is when lay people visit temples, keep extra precepts and hear teachings, and monastics gather to recite their training code.

o: five rules monks recite at the full moon
five sins that block the way to freedom
the five heaps a person seems to be made of

games.q: the five heaps, on the full-moon night: tap the pairs.
p: desire and lust for the heaps

s: the Buddha says the clinging and the heaps are the same thing
neither the same nor apart: the clinging is the desire and lust for the heaps.
MN 109 is set on the full-moon night of the fifteenth
the Buddha sits in the open air with the monks, and one stands to ask.
the Buddha answers the worry about not-self and deeds with questions
after a warning against trying to outrun the teaching, he asks: is body permanent? is what's impermanent worth calling me?

games.q: you're the monk on the full-moon night. you've asked what the heaps are rooted in. what does the Buddha say?
games.why: the five heaps that are clung to are rooted in desire. the elements support the body heap, but desire is the root of clinging.

practice: Picture an open night sky, and look lightly for the five heaps in yourself: a body sitting, a feeling pleasant or not, a sound you're naming, a small intention forming, and knowing underneath it all.
Don't grab any of them; let them be heaps under a wide sky.

wordCard.voice: Khandhas. The five heaps, body, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, that a monk asked the Buddha about on the full-moon night, learning the clinging is the grabbing, not the heaps.

orig.note: Pali khandha: heap, bundle, mass. Sanskrit skandha. the five heaps are what a person seems to be made of.

carryVoice: Your line: the clinging is the grabbing. The heaps are only heaps. That's the week.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 109, Mahapunnama Sutta (the great discourse on the full-moon night)
